header.title: De Vita Sancti Martini: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Paulinus Petricordiae
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's stoa0224b.stoa001.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's CSEL (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.

notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0224b.stoa001.opp-l: The speech in 194–203 is that of the lamenting voice introduced in the preceding lines. 'titulus' means a false title of honour in 195, but Martin's glorious deeds in 211 and 222. 'plangendis manibus' (194) is taken as dative, 'upon shades that should be mourned'.

nodes.text: ‘Let the ancient error cease, upon shades that should be mourned,
to add punishment, by giving them a title not their own,
lest one for whom the penalties of his crime alone are enough
should have this burden grow, doubled by an added honour.
And would that the saints, to whom by right is rendered this
homage, would deign to sprinkle with a slender drop our
unceasing flames, the fires of the wretched!
They, rejoicing, enjoy perpetual light;
us a dreadful chaos has hedged in with eternal gloom.
Far from the deserts of light is the confusion of night.’
This voice reached the ears of many far and wide,
but the form was revealed to Martin alone, whose
lighter mind passed through the weight of frail flesh,
seeing through the bodily mass by the light of the heart.
At once the altar is removed, and driven out is all
the empty superstition that had counterfeited sacred rites.
The mysteries, transferred, pass over to true worship.
What, after all, comparable to these glories will be able to offer
an art tainted with magic tricks or steeped in poisons,
weaving lying spells in contrived words
and probing stinking entrails with their veins inspected,
so that through the sought-out silences of Tartarean night
a mad demon may bellow with deceiving murmur,
taking on a feigned face under a thin image?
Here, surely, a simple soul and the devotion alone of one
at prayer undid the bonds of the law below,
and though the limbs were pressed by the weight of the tomb,
yet for that present time the confession lived.
Nor indeed is this the end of his glories, nor, broken off
even for a brief time, does the chain of his miracles cease.
